newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - Prodi seeks end to metalworkers' dispute.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Prodi seeks end to metalworkers' dispute.

text.p: A bitter pay dispute in Italy's key engineering and metalworking industry appeared to move closer to a settlement on Monday after Prime Minister Romano Prodi met labour and business leaders to try to break the deadlock.

The talks at Prodi's office were accompanied by an announcement by the sector employers' group Federmeccanica that it would meet unions during the day to resume talks for the first time in several months.

"We will be sitting down to see if we can reach a deal," Federmeccanica director general Michele Figurati told reporters. He said the talks would take place at the Labour Ministry with the leaders of the industry unions FIOM, FIM and UILM.

The protracted dispute, which has been accompanied by three one-day strikes since it began six months ago, affects 1.7 million workers in a sector which accounts for 40 percent of Italy's industrial output.
Any deal is likely to set the tone for other pay settlements and prove key to Italy's hopes of keeping a lid on inflation.
"There is a growing willingness to reach an agreement," Labour Minister Tiziano Treu told Italian radio. "It seems to me that we can go forward if we show goodwill."

Prodi's meeting was with the leaders of Italy's three main trades union confederations, CGIL, CISL and UIL, and the employers' umbrella organisation Confindustria. It ended after one hour with Figurati's announcement.
Prodi called the talks last Friday after signs of an end to deadlock over wage levels for the 1996-1998 contract period that has persisted since the previous agreement expired last June.
"Tomorrow is the start of the last round," Prodi told reporters on Sunday. "I think all the elements are in place to get ready to sign."

The dispute centres on differing interpretations of a landmark 1993 accord between the labour confederations, Confindustria and the government that ended a system of automatic inflation-linked wage increases.

Unions in the industry, which includes Italy's biggest company Fiat, initially sought a 230,000 lire ($144) a month rise to compensate for lost purchasing power but accepted a government proposal of 200,000 lire in December.
Federmeccanica has stuck to its original offer of 139,000 lire, arguing that any more would raise labour costs and fuel inflation, now running at about 2.6 percent year-on-year.
Prodi has insisted the government's compromise proposal is not inflationary.

It was not clear how the gap between the positions could be bridged but Italian media have reported that one option would be to lengthen the contract period a settlement would cover from two years to 30 months.
Unions have also shown a readiness to strike a deal.
"We are all committed and all the elements are there in order to square the circle tomorrow," Raffaele Morese, a senior official of the UIL labour confederation, said on Sunday. ($1=1595 Lire)
